chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid from his father from Abdullah ibn Bukayr from Zurara from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Samura ibn Junayd (may Allah curse him) had a date palm in the garden of a man from the Ansar. The Ansari's house was at the gate of the garden, and he would pass by it to go to his palm tree, but he did not ask for permission. The Ansari asked him to ask for permission when he came, but Samura refused. When he refused, the Ansari went to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and complained to him, informing him of the matter. The Messenger of Allah sent to him and informed him of what the Ansari had said and complained about, and said, 'When you want to enter, ask for permission.' He refused. When he refused, the Ansari bargained with him until he reached the price that Allah willed, but he refused to sell. The Ansari said, 'For it, you will have a date palm in Paradise.' He refused to accept. Then the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to the Ansari, 'Go, uproot it and throw it to him, for there is no harm and no causing harm.'

key_terms.عَذْقٌ مُذَلَّلٌ: A date palm (specifically one that yields fruit easily)
key_terms.لَا ضَرَرَ وَ لَا ضِرَارَ: There is no harm and no causing harm (a fundamental legal maxim)

ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling on entering someone's property without permission according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Prophet’s practical application of the maxim 'no harm and no causing harm' (la darara wa la dirar) in resolving property disputes, specifically regarding easement rights and entry into private gardens. It highlights the legal principle that persistent refusal to grant reasonable access or permission can lead to the forfeiture of the offending party's property rights as a form of compensation. The narrative underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on balancing individual ownership with communal convenience and preventing undue hardship.
